findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is in plain words. But this is the only paragraph about Athena itself. It never says why someone would pick it over other coding agents, or which AI models or accounts it needs.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page sits at Athena's address, yet almost all of it describes a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets three opening paragraphs on Athena and then a long technical study of someone else's tool.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: The page names two jobs: Athena turns requests into code changes, and it also writes studies. It never says how the two are connected, so a newcomer may not see why the study shows that the code-change product works.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim"

findings.text: The next steps are concrete, and a link near the top jumps to them. But they leave out what to install first (for example a Rust toolchain or AI API keys) and which repository the example request acts on. A newcomer would have to go to the GitHub repo to find this.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The firstmate explanation starts well. A one-sentence definition comes first, then a 'Words used first' list, then one task followed from start to finish, so a reader can follow the main flow.
findings.source: Start here: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker, so that several tasks can run side by side."

findings.text: The page is honest about what its sources leave unsaid, here and under 'Limits of this study'. Still, a central part of the yolo merge rule stays undefined for the reader.
findings.source: dt "in scope": "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: The States and Counters lists give only names, tags and ids such as t9, with no description on the same line. A newcomer has to look in the Transitions cards or the Glossary to understand them.
findings.source: States of a piece of work: "ready waiting" and Counters: "changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: Many definitions appear twice, word for word or nearly so, and some limits are stated three times: in Start here, on a transition card and in the claims. This makes an already dense page longer.
findings.source: Glossary entries for captain, yolo, green, red, home, in scope, compared with the 'Words used first' list

findings.text: These sections use Athena's internal terms ('job', 'recorded boundary', the 'studies/' folder) without explaining them, so they mean little to a first-time visitor.
findings.source: Limits of this study f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate" and About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"

findings.text: Every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to exact file lines at a pinned commit. This is a concrete demonstration of the traceability the opening promises.
findings.source: Next steps: "Check a statement: follow a bracketed claim id to the claim, then its source link to the file and lines in firstmate at the pinned commit."
